claims.text: Short-range chemical ordering occurs at or near grain boundaries in high-entropy nanoalloys at elevated temperatures.
Boundary-associated short-range chemical ordering is the primary governor of structural and chemical stability in high-entropy nanoalloys at elevated temperatures.
Short-range chemical ordering reduces grain-boundary mobility.
Short-range chemical ordering suppresses elemental segregation.
The proposed starting films are nanocrystalline, with average grain sizes below 100 nm.
The proposed starting films have minimal segregation and a uniform elemental distribution.
Nanoscale short-range ordering near grain boundaries inhibits local atomic diffusion paths.
Atomic-scale ordering introduces an enthalpic barrier to grain-boundary motion.
The enthalpic barrier created by atomic-scale ordering retards elemental segregation at high temperature.
Retarded boundary motion stabilizes the microstructure and suppresses grain coarsening.
In-situ heated alloys with pronounced boundary ordering will show slower grain growth than ex-situ annealed references.
In-situ heated alloys with pronounced boundary ordering will show smaller compositional fluctuations than ex-situ annealed references.
In-situ heated alloys with pronounced boundary ordering will show less second-phase precipitation than ex-situ annealed references.
Without short-range ordering, otherwise identical high-temperature exposures will produce greater grain coarsening.
Without short-range ordering, otherwise identical high-temperature exposures will produce more severe segregation.
The prediction applies to initially homogeneous, nanocrystalline high-entropy alloys within single-phase stability regions near 1200 K.
Severe mechanical stress or extensive interfacial reactions can override the stabilization attributed to short-range ordering.
Above approximately 1200 K or in aggressive environments, bulk diffusion and external interactions may overshadow the effects of short-range ordering.
